title: Monic additive polynomial quotient of a proper additive subgroup, with scalar equivariance
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], and write $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$ and $\mathbf G_m(R)=R^\times$ on commutative $k$-algebras [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $N\subsetneq\mathbf G_a$ be a proper closed $k$-subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-weil-closed-immersion]. There is a unique monic polynomial $P\in k[T]$ of positive degree $n$ whose principal ideal is the defining ideal of $N$ in $k[T]$. It satisfies $P(0)=0$ and $P(X+Y)=P(X)+P(Y)$ in $k[X,Y]$. The morphism $P:\mathbf G_a\to\mathbf G_a$ defined on $R$-points by $x\mapsto P(x)$ is a faithfully flat finitely presented group-scheme homomorphism with scheme-theoretic kernel $N$, and induces an isomorphism from the fppf sheaf quotient $\mathbf G_a/N$ to $\mathbf G_a$. Here faithfully flat means that the coordinate-ring map makes its target a faithfully flat module over its source, and the quotient is the sheafification of $R\mapsto R/N(R)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. If $G$ is an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], $\eta:G\to\mathbf G_m$ is a homomorphism, and scalar multiplication through $\eta$ preserves $N$ on all $k$-algebras, then
$$P(\eta_R(g)x)=\eta_R(g)^nP(x)$$
for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, $g\in G(R)$, and $x\in R$. Thus the induced action on the displayed quotient is the scalar action through $\eta^n$.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; endomorphisms of the additive group in 14.40; the equivariant exact sequence used in Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The monic normalization gives the quotient character eta^n by comparison of leading coefficients.

proof.text:
By the affine description of a closed immersion, write $N=\operatorname{Spec}(k[T]/I)$ inside $\mathbf G_a=\operatorname{Spec}k[T]$. Properness gives $I
e0$. The identity belongs to $N(k)$, so every member of $I$ vanishes at $0$; hence $I
e k[T]$. Apply the polynomial principal-ideal-domain lemma to obtain $I=(f)$ with $f
e0$, and divide $f$ by its nonzero leading coefficient to get a monic generator $P$. A constant monic generator would be $1$, contradicting $I
e k[T]$, so $n=\deg P\ge1$; also $P(0)=0$. If $Q$ is another monic generator, write $Q=AP$ and $P=BQ$. Cancellation gives $AB=1$. Degrees of nonzero polynomial products add over the field, so $A,B$ are constants, and monicity gives $A=B=1$. Thus $P$ is unique.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; Example 14.40, printed pp.292–293; Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The following coefficient arguments supply the exercise and the scalar normalization.

proof.text: Set $D(X,Y)=P(X+Y)-P(X)-P(Y)$. Expansion of the powers shows that every surviving monomial has both $X$-exponent and $Y$-exponent strictly below $n$: the pure powers cancel, and $P(0)=0$. Put $A=k[X]/(P(X))$ and $B=A[Y]/(P(Y))$. If $x,y\in B$ are the two distinguished roots, then $P(x)=P(y)=0$, so $x,y\in N(B)$. The subgroup condition on all $k$-algebras gives $x+y\in N(B)$, hence $D(x,y)=0$. By the monic-quotient basis lemma over $A$, all coefficients of $D(x,Y)$ in the powers $1,y,\ldots,y^{n-1}$ are zero in $A$. Each such coefficient comes from a polynomial in $X$ of degree below $n$, so the same basis lemma over $k$ makes every one of its coefficients zero. Thus $D=0$ in $k[X,Y]$.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; Example 14.40, printed pp.292–293; Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The following coefficient arguments supply the exercise and the scalar normalization.

proof.text: The coordinate homomorphism $k[U]\to k[T]$, $U\mapsto P(T)$, defines the required morphism $q:\mathbf G_a\to\mathbf G_a$. The polynomial identity just proved gives $q_R(x+y)=q_R(x)+q_R(y)$ for every $k$-algebra $R$, so it is a group-scheme homomorphism. Pulling back the zero section imposes the equation $P(T)=0$, giving $\ker q=\operatorname{Spec}k[T]/(P)=N$ as a closed subgroup scheme, including its scheme structure.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; Example 14.40, printed pp.292–293; Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The following coefficient arguments supply the exercise and the scalar normalization.

proof.text: Put $C=k[U]$ and $E=C[T]/(P(T)-U)$. Evaluation $U\mapsto P(T)$ induces $E\to k[T]$; the reverse map sends $T$ to its class. They are inverse: they fix $T$, and in $E$ the class of $U$ equals $P(T)$. This is an isomorphism of $C$-algebras when $k[T]$ has structure map $U\mapsto P(T)$. The relation is monic in $T$ of degree $n\ge1$. Apply the monic-quotient faithful-tensor-coordinate lemma with base ring $C$ and degree $n$. It gives both the basis $1,T,\ldots,T^{n-1}$ and faithful flatness of $C\to k[T]$. The same presentation, with one generator and one relation, is a finite presentation of this algebra.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; Example 14.40, printed pp.292–293; Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The following coefficient arguments supply the exercise and the scalar normalization.

proof.text: By the affine flatness criterion $q$ is flat, and faithful flatness gives surjectivity of its spectrum map. The explicit presentation in the preceding step gives local finite presentation on the displayed affine chart. It also shows that $q$ is finite: over a principal open $D(h)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}C$ the inverse-image ring is $C_h[T]/(P(T)-U)$ with the same finite basis, so its section module is finite locally on the target, as required by the affine definition of finiteness. Thus $q$ is finite, flat and locally of finite presentation, hence finite locally free. For completeness it is globally of finite presentation: a map between these affine schemes is affine and quasi-compact, and is separated (therefore quasi-separated); combine this with local finite presentation.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; Example 14.40, printed pp.292–293; Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The following coefficient arguments supply the exercise and the scalar normalization.

proof.text: For the translation relation take $R_0=N\times_k\mathbf G_a$ with $s(z,x)=x$ and $t(z,x)=x+z$. Its map to $\mathbf G_a\times_{q,\mathbf G_a,q}\mathbf G_a$ is $(z,x)\mapsto(x,x+z)$, with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(y-x,x)$: indeed additivity gives $P(y-x)=P(y)-P(x)=0$. These formulas are polynomial maps on the displayed closed subschemes and their composites are identities. Apply the finite-locally-free kernel-pair quotient lemma with base $\operatorname{Spec}k$, $U=M=\mathbf G_a$, and this $R_0$. All its hypotheses now hold, so $q$ identifies $\mathbf G_a$ with the fppf sheafification of $H\mapsto\mathbf G_a(H)/N(H)$. On affine tests $H=\operatorname{Spec}R$ this is exactly $R\mapsto R/N(R)$ as in the statement. The isomorphism preserves addition since $q$ does.

source.place: Exercise 14-3(a), printed p.301; Example 14.40, printed pp.292–293; Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319. The following coefficient arguments supply the exercise and the scalar normalization.

proof.text: Fix a $k$-algebra $R$ and $g\in G(R)$, and put $a=\eta_R(g)\in R^\times$. In $B=R[T]/(P(T))$ let $t$ be the distinguished root and let $g_B$ be the image of $g$ by the structure map. Since $t\in N(B)$, the assumed scalar stability on all $k$-algebras gives $at\in N(B)$ and hence $P(at)=0$. The polynomial $Q(T)=P(aT)-a^nP(T)$ has zero $T^n$ coefficient and therefore degree below $n$. Its image in $B$ is zero. The monic-quotient basis lemma over $R$ makes all its coefficients zero, even when $R$ has nilpotents or is the zero ring. Evaluating $Q=0$ at any $x\in R$ gives $P(ax)=a^nP(x)$. Consequently the quotient isomorphism of the preceding step intertwines the action through $\eta$ with multiplication through $\eta^n$.
